statement: To find two medial straight lines commensurable in square only, containing a rational rectangle, and such that the square on the greater is greater than the square on the less by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with the greater.
heath_proof: Let there be set out two rational straight lines A, B commensurable in square only and such that the square on A, being the greater, is greater than the square on B the less by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with A. [X. 29] And let the square on C be equal to the rectangle A, B. Now the rectangle A, B is medial; [X. 21] therefore the square on C is also medial; therefore C is also medial. [X. 21] Let the rectangle C, D be equal to the square on B. Now the square on B is rational; therefore the rectangle C, D is also rational. And since, as A is to B, so is the rectangle A, B to the square on B, while the square on C is equal to the rectangle A, B, and the rectangle C, D is equal to the square on B, therefore, as A is to B, so is the square on C to the rectangle C, D. But, as the square on C is to the rectangle C, D, so is C to D; therefore also, as A is to B, so is C to D. But A is commensurable with B in square only; therefore C is also commensurable with D in square only. [X. 11] And C is medial; therefore D is also medial. [X. 23, addition] And since, as A is to B, so is C to D, and the square on A is greater than the square on B by the square on a straight line commensurable with A, therefore also the square on C is greater than the square on D by the square on a straight line commensurable with C. [X. 14] Therefore two medial straight lines C, D, commensurable in square only and containing a rational rectangle, have been found, and the square on C is greater than the square on D by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with C. Similarly also it can be proved that the square on C exceeds the square on D by the square on a straight line incommensurable with C, when the square on A is greater than the square on B by the square on a straight line incommensurable with A. [X. 30]

**Statement:** To find two medial straight lines commensurable in square only, containing a rational rectangle, and such that the square on the greater is greater than the square on the less by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with the greater.

**Step 1.** By Proposition 10.29, find two rational straight lines A and B, commensurable in square only, with A greater than B, such that the square on A is greater than the square on B by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with A.

**Step 2.** By Proposition 6.13, take C as a mean proportional between A and B, so that A is to C as C is to B, and the square on C equals the rectangle contained by A and B.

**Step 3.** Since A and B are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, by Proposition 10.21 the rectangle contained by A and B is irrational, and the side of the square equal to it is medial. Since the square on C equals this rectangle, C is medial.

**Step 4.** By Proposition 6.12, take D as the fourth proportional to A, B, C, so that A is to B as C is to D.

**Step 5.** We show that D is medial. From A is to B as C is to D, by Proposition 6.22, the square on A is to the square on B as the square on C is to the square on D. Now since A and B are rational, the squares on A and on B are both rational areas, hence both are commensurable with the square on the assigned rational straight line, and therefore commensurable with each other by Proposition 10.12. Since the square on A is commensurable with the square on B, and the square on A is to the square on B as the square on C is to the square on D, by Proposition 10.11 the square on C is commensurable with the square on D.

**Step 6.** Let R be a rational straight line. Apply the square on C to R, producing breadth V, so that the rectangle contained by R and V equals the square on C. Since C is medial, by Proposition 10.22, V is rational and incommensurable in length with R.

**Step 7.** Apply the square on D to R, producing breadth W, so that the rectangle contained by R and W equals the square on D. Since the square on C is to the square on D as the rectangle R by V is to the rectangle R by W, by Proposition 6.1 this ratio equals V to W. Since the square on C is commensurable with the square on D (Step 5), by Proposition 10.11, V is commensurable with W.

**Step 8.** Since V is rational and W is commensurable with V, by Proposition 10.12, W is rational. Since V is incommensurable in length with R and W is commensurable with V, by Proposition 10.13, W is incommensurable in length with R. Therefore R and W are rational straight lines commensurable in square only.

**Step 9.** By Proposition 10.21, the rectangle contained by R and W is irrational and the side of the square equal to it is medial. Since the rectangle R by W equals the square on D, D is medial.

**Step 10.** We show that C and D are commensurable in square only. From Step 5, the square on C is commensurable with the square on D, so C and D are commensurable in square. Since A is to B as C is to D (Step 4), and A and B are incommensurable in length (being commensurable in square only), by Proposition 10.11, C and D are incommensurable in length. Therefore C and D are commensurable in square only.

**Step 11.** We show that the rectangle contained by C and D is rational. From Step 2, A is to C as C is to B (C being the mean proportional of A and B). From Step 4, A is to B as C is to D. By Proposition 5.16 (alternando), A is to C as B is to D. Since A is to C as C is to B, we have C is to B as B is to D. Therefore B is the mean proportional between C and D, and by Proposition 6.17, the rectangle contained by C and D equals the square on B. Since B is rational, the square on B is a rational area by Definition 10.1.4. Hence the rectangle contained by C and D is rational.

**Step 12.** We show that the square on C is greater than the square on D by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with C. We have A is to B as C is to D, and the square on A is greater than the square on B by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with A (Step 1). By Proposition 10.14, the square on C is greater than the square on D by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with C.

**Step 13.** Therefore C and D are two medial straight lines commensurable in square only, containing a rational rectangle, such that the square on the greater is greater than the square on the less by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with the greater. This is what was required to find.
